passage.sceneTitle: The Horse Who Would Not Cross the Bridge
passage.preamble: Black Beauty is a horse, and he tells his own story. Here he is pulling a light open carriage called a dog-cart, taking his master and John the groom to town and home again on a wet, windy autumn day.

numberedLines.text: One day late in the autumn my master had a long journey to go on business. I was put
into the dog-cart, and John went with his master. I always liked to go in the dog-cart,
it was so light and the high wheels ran along so pleasantly. There had been a great deal
of rain, and now the wind was very high and blew the dry leaves across the road in a
shower. We went along merrily till we came to the toll-bar and the low wooden bridge.
The river banks were rather high, and the bridge, instead of rising, went across just
level, so that in the middle, if the river was full, the water would be nearly up to the
woodwork and planks; but as there were good substantial rails on each side, people did
not mind it.
The man at the gate said the river was rising fast, and he feared it would be a bad
night. Many of the meadows were under water, and in one low part of the road the water
was halfway up to my knees; the bottom was good, and master drove gently, so it was no
matter.
When we got to the town of course I had a good bait, but as the master's business
engaged him a long time we did not start for home till rather late in the afternoon. The
wind was then much higher, and I heard the master say to John that he had never been out
in such a storm; and so I thought, as we went along the skirts of a wood, where the
great branches were swaying about like twigs, and the rushing sound was terrible.
“I wish we were well out of this wood,” said my master.
“Yes, sir,” said John, “it would be rather awkward if one of these branches came down
upon us.”
The words were scarcely out of his mouth when there was a groan, and a crack, and a
splitting sound, and tearing, crashing down among the other trees came an oak, torn up
by the roots, and it fell right across the road just before us. I will never say I was
not frightened, for I was. I stopped still, and I believe I trembled; of course I did
not turn round or run away; I was not brought up to that. John jumped out and was in a
moment at my head.
“That was a very near touch,” said my master. “What's to be done now?”
“Well, sir, we can't drive over that tree, nor yet get round it; there will be nothing
for it, but to go back to the four crossways, and that will be a good six miles before
we get round to the wooden bridge again; it will make us late, but the horse is fresh.”
So back we went and round by the crossroads, but by the time we got to the bridge it was
very nearly dark; we could just see that the water was over the middle of it; but as
that happened sometimes when the floods were out, master did not stop. We were going
along at a good pace, but the moment my feet touched the first part of the bridge I felt
sure there was something wrong. I dare not go forward, and I made a dead stop. “Go on,
Beauty,” said my master, and he gave me a touch with the whip, but I dare not stir; he
gave me a sharp cut; I jumped, but I dare not go forward.
“There's something wrong, sir,” said John, and he sprang out of the dog-cart and came to
my head and looked all about. He tried to lead me forward. “Come on, Beauty, what's the
matter?” Of course I could not tell him, but I knew very well that the bridge was not
safe.
Just then the man at the toll-gate on the other side ran out of the house, tossing a
torch about like one mad.
“Hoy, hoy, hoy! halloo! stop!” he cried.
“What's the matter?” shouted my master.
“The bridge is broken in the middle, and part of it is carried away; if you come on
you'll be into the river.”
“Thank God!” said my master. “You Beauty!” said John, and took the bridle and gently
turned me round to the right-hand road by the river side. The sun had set some time; the
wind seemed to have lulled off after that furious blast which tore up the tree. It grew
darker and darker, stiller and stiller. I trotted quietly along, the wheels hardly
making a sound on the soft road. For a good while neither master nor John spoke, and
then master began in a serious voice. I could not understand much of what they said, but
I found they thought, if I had gone on as the master wanted me, most likely the bridge
would have given way under us, and horse, chaise, master, and man would have fallen into
the river; and as the current was flowing very strongly, and there was no light and no
help at hand, it was more than likely we should all have been drowned.
We saw a light at the hall-door and at the upper windows, and as we came up mistress ran
out, saying, “Are you really safe, my dear? Oh! I have been so anxious, fancying all
sorts of things. Have you had no accident?”
“No, my dear; but if your Black Beauty had not been wiser than we were we should all
have been carried down the river at the wooden bridge.”

stem.text: Why did Beauty like going in the dog-cart? (lines 2 and 3)

rows.key: It was light, and its high wheels ran along pleasantly.

options.value: It was light, and its high wheels ran along pleasantly.
It was the only cart he was strong enough to pull.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A reason a child may supply; the passage gives lightness as the cart's quality, not his.

options.value: It meant John came with him instead of the master.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Takes a true detail from the SAME sentence, line 2, but not the one that answers why.

options.value: It was slow, so the journey felt easy.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: Differs by one word: line 3 says light, not slow.

rows.hintCore: One sentence gives two reasons together.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 2 and 3. Beauty says the dog-cart was so light. He says the high wheels ran along so pleasantly. Those two things are his reason.

stem.text: Read lines 6 to 8. Line 8 says the bridge had 'good substantial rails'. What does 'substantial' mean here?

options.value: Very large in amount.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: The commonest other sense of the word, which a pair of rails does not fit.

options.value: Strong and solidly built.
Newly put up that year.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing gives the rails an age; line 8 is about what they are like.

options.value: Painted so they could be seen.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses the idea of good rails as a warning; the line is about how they are made.

rows.hintCore: Ask what would make people not mind the water.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 6 to 8. The bridge sits level, so floodwater can reach the planks. The rails are what stop people minding it. Rails that do that have to be strongly built.

stem.text: What did the man at the gate say about the river? (lines 10 and 11)

rows.key: It was rising fast, and he feared a bad night.

options.value: It had already broken the wooden bridge.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Takes the news from line 47, which arrives hours later.

options.value: It was falling now that the rain had stopped.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Reverses rising; line 4 also says there had been a great deal of rain.

options.value: It was rising fast, and he feared a bad night.
It had covered the meadows so the road was shut.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 11 says meadows were under water, but nothing says the road was shut.

rows.hintCore: He says two things: what is happening, and what he fears.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 10 and 11. The man says the river was rising fast. He says he feared it would be a bad night. The broken bridge is not known until much later.

stem.text: In town Beauty says 'I had a good bait'. What does 'bait' mean here? (line 14)

options.value: Something used to catch a fish.
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: The commonest other sense of the word, which this sentence does not fix.

options.value: A long wait outside, with nothing to eat.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 14 calls it a GOOD bait, which a wait with nothing to eat could not be.

options.value: A trick played to make him go on.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Invents a purpose; nothing in the line suggests he was tricked.

options.value: A feed and a rest.

rows.hintCore: Ask what a horse would be given, not a fisherman.
rows.walkScript: Look at line 14. Beauty is a horse who has pulled a cart to town. What a horse is given on arriving is food and rest. That is what a good bait means here.

stem.text: What came down across the road in front of them? (lines 22 to 24)

rows.key: An oak tree, torn up by the roots.

options.value: An oak tree, torn up by the roots.
A great branch from one of the swaying trees.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: Line 20 names a branch as John's worry; line 23 says a whole oak came down.

options.value: Part of the wooden bridge, carried off by the flood.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: Takes the bridge damage from line 47, which happens elsewhere and later.

options.value: A shower of dry leaves blown across the road.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: True of line 4, at the start of the journey, not here. In the window, line 22 answers the stem: 'The words were scarcely out of his mouth when'.

rows.hintCore: The sounds come before the thing is named.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 22 to 24. The sounds come first: a groan, a crack, a splitting. Then line 23 names what made them. It was an oak, torn up by the roots.

stem.text: Beauty says he did not turn round or run away. Why not? (lines 24 to 26)

rows.key: He had been trained not to, even when frightened.

options.value: He was not frightened by the falling tree.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 24 says the opposite: he will never say he was not frightened.

options.value: He had been trained not to, even when frightened.
The dog-cart was too heavy to turn on the road.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A sensible guess, but the passage gives his training as the reason.

options.value: John was already holding him at his head.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: John reaches his head at line 26, after Beauty has already stopped still.

rows.hintCore: He tells you he was frightened first. Read on.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 24 to 26. Beauty says plainly that he was frightened. Then he says he did not turn or run. He was not brought up to that.

stem.text: What did John say they would have to do? (lines 29 to 31)

rows.key: Go back to the crossways and round, six miles further.

options.value: Drive slowly over the tree where it lay lowest.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Line 29 says they cannot drive over it, nor get round it.

options.value: Wait by the wood until the storm had passed.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A reasonable plan, but not the one John gives.

options.value: Go back to the crossways and round, six miles further.
Unhitch Beauty and lead him home on foot.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Invents an action; line 31 says the horse is fresh, so they drive on.

rows.hintCore: He says what they cannot do before what they will do.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 29 to 31. John says they cannot go over the tree or round it. So they turn back to the four crossways. That adds a good six miles to the way home.

stem.text: Water was over the middle of the bridge. Why did the master not stop? (lines 33 and 34)

rows.key: Because that had happened before in floods.

options.value: Because it was too dark for him to see the water.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 33 says they could just see the water, so he did see it.

options.value: Because the gatekeeper had waved them across.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: The gatekeeper does run out, but at line 43, to stop them, not to wave them on.

options.value: Because Beauty was going at a good pace and could not stop.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 34's good pace; line 36 has Beauty making a dead stop of his own.

options.value: Because that had happened before in floods.

rows.hintCore: A short clause in line 34 carries the reason.
rows.walkScript: Look at line 34. The clause says that happened sometimes when the floods were out. So the master had seen water on the bridge before. He read it as usual, not as danger.

stem.text: Look at what the master does on the bridge. Then look at what he says at the hall door. What does the writer want us to understand? (lines 36 to 38 and 62 to 63)

rows.key: The master punished Beauty for the very thing that saved them.

options.value: The master punished Beauty for the very thing that saved them.
The master knew that Beauty was right to stop on the bridge.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Reverses lines 37 and 38, where he gives a touch and then a sharp cut to force him on.

options.value: Beauty was too frightened of the water to cross the bridge.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Line 41 says he knew the bridge was not safe, so it is knowledge, not fear.

options.value: The master had wanted to test whether Beauty would obey him at all.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Invents a purpose; line 37 has him simply telling Beauty to go on.

rows.hintCore: Two places, far apart, are about the same moment of refusing.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 37 and 38 first. The master gives a touch, then a sharp cut. Now look at lines 62 and 63: he calls the horse wiser than they were. The refusal he punished is the one he later thanks.

stem.text: Read lines 50 to 52. Line 52 says it grew 'darker and darker, stiller and stiller'. Why does the writer write it that way?
quotes: darker and darker, stiller and stiller

rows.key: To make the change feel slow and steady.

options.value: To show the storm was still getting worse.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Line 51 says the wind had lulled, so the storm is easing, not worsening.

options.value: To make the change feel slow and steady.
To show Beauty was growing tired at the end of the day.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Gives the horse the evening's quality; the lines describe the dark and the quiet.

options.value: To copy the sound of the wheels on the soft road.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 52's wheels, which are mentioned for their quietness, not their sound.

rows.hintCore: Ask what saying a word twice does to time.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 50 to 52. The wind has lulled and the wheels hardly make a sound. Then two pairs of words repeat: darker and darker, stiller and stiller. Saying each one twice makes the change feel gradual.

stem.text: What did the master and John work out on the way home? (lines 54 to 58)

rows.key: That going on would probably have drowned them all.

options.value: That Beauty had been badly trained and needed more work.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Reverses the sense; line 55 has them crediting the horse for stopping.

options.value: That the gatekeeper was to blame for the broken bridge.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Invents a complaint; the passage gives them no blame at all.

options.value: That going on would probably have drowned them all.
That they were lucky the wind had lulled when it did.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: The lull is real at line 51, but it is not what they are said to be thinking about.

rows.hintCore: Follow the chain of ifs to where it ends.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 55 to 58. They think the bridge would have given way under them. Then they think what the current and the dark would have meant. Their conclusion is that they would most likely all have drowned.

stem.text: Beauty repeats what the people say, word for word. What does the writer keep reminding us at the same time?

rows.key: He gives us their words exactly, but says he cannot follow them.

options.value: That Beauty is too frightened to listen properly.
options.tagChildHint: Pick the word you can prove from the text. Close is not the same.
options.execution: Swaps the evidenced limit, understanding, for a feeling the passage does not give.

options.value: That the people never speak to Beauty at all.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Reads past the fact that they do speak to him, at lines 36, 40 and 49.

options.value: That Beauty repeats the words to show off what he knows.
options.tagChildHint: A reason has to be given, not guessed. Ask what the text says about why.
options.execution: Invents a motive; the narrator's remarks are about what he cannot do, not what he can.

options.value: He gives us their words exactly, but says he cannot follow them.

rows.hintCore: Notice what he says about the talking, not what is said.
rows.walkScript: Beauty gives you whole speeches, at lines 19, 28 and 47. At line 41 he says he could not tell John. At line 54 he says he could not understand much. He hands you the words and stands outside them.

stem.text: Beauty says 'I dare not stir'. What does 'stir' mean here? (lines 36 to 38)

options.value: Move at all.
Mix something round and round.
options.tagChildHint: Swap your word into the sentence — does it still mean the same thing?

options.value: Make any sound.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.

options.value: Wake up from a doze.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.

rows.hintCore: The words around it are all about going forward.
rows.walkScript: Look at lines 36 to 38. Beauty makes a dead stop and will not go forward. Then he jumps at the sharp cut, but still does not go on. So 'stir' here is about moving.
